name: Gizey
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: De Dominicis, Amedeo. 2008. Phonological sketch of Gizey. Studi Linguistici e Filologici Online 6: 1-78. Pisa: Dipartimento di Linguistica, Universita di Pisa (ISSN 1724-5230). Open PDF (the Internet Archive capture 2018-04-22 of www.humnet.unipi.it/slifo/vol6/).
catalog_quote: Gizey is an unwritten tonal language. [...] For a full description of the tonal system of Gizey, refer to De Dominicis (2007). [p. 74] 4. The Tones. Gizey is a tonal language. Experimental findings (De Dominicis 2007) demonstrate the linguistic function of two tonal registers (H and L). Particularly, the H/L tones oppose some minimal pairs both lexically and grammatically. [p. 75] In the former case, a list of nouns opposed according to tone has been identified; in the latter case, the tonal opposition expresses the verbal aspect (accomplished/unaccomplished). This tonal function occurs in many languages belonging to central Chadic branch, such as for instance, Masa. Nevertheless, field research (De Dominicis 2007) has allowed us to verify the weak functional load had by tonal oppositions in Gizey[20]. As a consequence, it can be argued that linguistic tones in Gizey play a minor linguistic function and are probably destined to disappear, as their tonal system is endangered. [fn 20] But only few minimal pairs were found in the lexicon. And in identification and discrimination tests Gizey speakers often misunderstand and do not recognize tonal oppositions.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only full phonological description of Gizey treats it as a two-register (H/L) tone language with lexical and aspectual tonal contrasts of weak functional load; it contains no statement about word stress or accent at all (the words 'stress'/'accent' appear only in bibliography titles). No opened source locates a word stress in Gizey.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the sketch notes roots are maximally disyllabic (compounds, ideophones, toponyms, loans excepted) but says nothing about prominence.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology (roots, suffixed nouns, verbs) and tone; De Dominicis 2010 treats intonation-phrase prominences ('sentence stress') only as a general concept, not as a Gizey word-stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1/5.3 gize1234 is a language-level languoid (NOCODE_Gizey) in the Masa section beside Masana [masa1322]; Glottolog also lists 'Gizay' [giza1238] as a dialect of Masana, and Ethnologue folds Gizey into Masana [mcn]. De Dominicis' data are from Djougoumta (Mayo-Danay, Guéré, Far North Cameroon; 10 speakers); Ajello 2005 and Guitang 2021 treat Gizey as a distinct language not mutually intelligible with Masa. The Masa-language check (masa1322) had already filed De Dominicis' Gizey tone papers under Masa; they belong here.

new_statements.quote: Words in Gizey are generally monosyllabic or disyllabic. Ideophones also abide by this constraint. [...] As for tone, the tonal schemes occurring in ideophones are L (e.g., kìrèɗ 'associated with sliding', dà 'directly', pèŋgèfì 'small'), H (e.g., híʤíp [...], tíníŋníŋ 'huge quantity', ɗít 'violently'), LH (e.g., dùrlú 'vast', bìgímgím 'loud sound of water') and HL (e.g., kéɓèrèɗ 'describing very small ears', kégéglèkgè 'cock-a-doodle-do', ʧálàl 'well, clearly'). These lexically specified tonal patterns also occur elsewhere in the lexicon. In Gizey, it is mostly verbs that have clearly predictable tonal patterns (see, e.g. De Dominicis 2006; Guitang 2024).

new_statements.relation_note: Silent on stress but refines the tone description: four lexical tonal schemes (L, H, LH, HL) for nouns/ideophones, verbs with predictable tone, polysyllabic words tending to be monotonal (about 65 % of CV.CVC noun roots). Consistent with the catalog's tone language, no stress statement reading from De Dominicis 2008.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gizey is described as a tone language with lexically specified tonal schemes L, H, LH, HL on words (verbs having predictable tone). No word-stress or accent statement anywhere; the only prominence-type remarks concern 'foregrounded prosody' (pause, pitch reset, amplitude rise, segmental lengthening) of ideophones as utterance-level depictive marking, not lexical stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Gizey as a Masa languoid of Cameroon and Chad (Glottocode gize1234, no ISO code, 10.02N 15.27E, about 12,000-19,000 speakers); Guitang 2021 notes it is often treated as a dialect of Masana (mcn) but argues for separate-language status, with asymmetric partial mutual intelligibility. No sub-dialect is singled out. Guitang's data come from his own fieldwork plus Melis' early-2000s material; De Dominicis' earlier data (the catalog source) come from Djougoumta.

tone_statements.citation: Guitang, Guillaume & Pius W. Akumbu. 2025. Gizey onomatopoeias. SKASE Journal of Theoretical Linguistics 22(2): 48-60. (HAL hal-05203918; ULB DI-fusion 2013/392762.)
tone_statements.quote: In Gizey, words tend to be lexically specified with different tonal schemes. For example, nouns generally select between Low-Low, Low-High, High-Low, and Low-High-Low tonal schemes (Guitang 2024). Onomatopoeias generally select between High, e.g., ɓát ‘sound when wood breaks’, ɓɛ́tɓɛ́t ‘sound when someone walks’, ʧíŋʧíŋʧíŋ ‘southern red bishop call’ and Low, e.g., dìm ‘sound of a big and heavy object thrown in water’, gìndìm ‘sound of a loud gun’. A Low-High scheme is found on a few onomatopoeias, e.g., ɲìgí ‘guinea fowl call’.
tone_statements.summary: 2 tone heights H, L combining into lexical schemes (nouns LL, LH, HL, LHL; onomatopoeias H or L, rarely LH).

tone.quote: Gizey is an unwritten, so far undescribed, tonal language. It is classified in the family of Chadic languages, one of the four families of the Afroasiatic phylum. Gizey belongs to the Biu-Mandara or the Masa branch, which includes two sections: Masa (Masa, Gizey) and Musey (Musey, Ham, Marba-Lew, Monogoy).

sources.note: 104-page book chapter devoted to Gizey tone (IRIS dc.subject 'Gizey; tone'); the fullest write-up of the author's first-hand analysis summarised in his TAL 2006 paper (the works listed here): two tonal levels H/L, falling contour on noun definiteness suffixes analysed as floating L + H, verbal aspect (perfective/imperfective) marked by tone, perception tests suggesting a weak functional load. Not opened.
